texts.orig: Developments in the additive manufacturing (AM) of titanium (Ti) alloys are critical for the aerospace industry because they have excellent properties  for  structural  applications,  such  as  high  specific  strength, good  creep  resistance,  good  fatigue  performance,  reasonable  weld­ ability, and excellent corrosion resistance [1 -4]. However, high material and manufacturing costs pose challenges to the further exploitation of Ti alloys  in  the  aerospace  industry  [5].  These  challenges  are  especially significant for conventional manufacturing methods where scrap ma­ terial can exceed 80% of the starting material [6,7]. Therefore, near-net production  with  reduced  material  waste,  geometric  freedom,  shorter lead  times,  and  reduced  energy  consumption  [8,9]  provided  by state-of-the-art AM technologies is seen as an attractive solution.

texts.orig: Recent developments in additive manufacturing (AM) have shown the importance of small-scale mechanical testing due to material availability issues, the microstructural variance within the complex build geometries, or thin-type features such as lattices. The current approach in AM is to test standard-sized coupons and postulate that a component with complex geometry has similar mechanical properties even though their thermal histories are completely different in many cases. In this research, small-scale tensile testing methodologies of AM parts made  by  electron  beam  wire-fed  (EB-WF)  deposited  Ti -6Al -4V  were  investigated.  Specifically,  specimens extracted  from  well-established  Ti -6Al -4V  microstructural  zones  of  transient  and  steady-state  regions  were compared to  understand  the  effect  of  local  microstructure  on  mechanical  properties,  which  were  evaluated through microhardness and miniature tensile testing. The average microhardness in the transient and steadystate zones are 321 Hv  and 306 Hv, respectively. Although distinct microstructural features were observed in these zones, their tensile properties were similar. Both deposited zones had tensile yield and ultimate strength values ranging between 825-832 MPa and 880 -907 MPa, respectively. The measured properties of the miniature specimens were comparable with E8 standard-sized specimens, higher than the ASTM F1108 cast and lower than the AMS 4911P wrought Ti -6Al -4V standards. Deformation and fractography analysis were used to correlate microstructure and property relationships for different α lath morphologies. Basket-weave morphology in the transient zone specimen showed profound grain splitting by basal slip which led to microstructural refinement and hindered softening during plastic flow.

texts.orig: Among many metals AM technologies [10 -15], a directed energy deposition (DED) technique, electron beam wire-fed (EB-WF) additive deposition -also  commercially  known  as  electron  beam  additive manufacturing (EBAM) [16 -19] -attracts attention for larger scale parts due to its high deposition rates (reaching up to kilograms per hour) and cost/safety  effectiveness  associated  with  the  use  of  wire  instead  of powder feedstock [20]. Similar to other wire-fed DED techniques, the feedstock wire is continuously fed into the moving melt pool during EBAM to build up the deposit geometry. EBAM generally employs travel speeds, melt pool sizes, and layer heights that range between 2 and 15 mm/s, 1 -10 mm wide, and 0.5 -2 mm, respectively [16,21 -23]. Due to these  processing  conditions,  the  solidification  front  velocity  (1 -10 mm/s) and cooling rates (10 2 K/s) [9,16] are considerably lower than those observed in laser (10 6 K/s) [24] or electron beam (10 5 K/s) [25]

texts.orig: Microstructural/property variance within the thermal cycle depen­ dent local zones is more evident for Ti alloys due to the allotropic phase transformations  [1,2].  Such  microstructural  variations  are  sequential and attributed to the moving heat source creating thermal profiles and cyclic heating and cooling steps. Multiple literature studies reported that cyclic thermal history creates regularly spaced 'layer bands ' in deposits of the widely studied Ti -6Al -4V alloy [7,9,26 -30]. Layer bands have been vaguely observed in PBF built Ti -6Al -4V coupons [31], but they are distinctively more visible in wire-fed [32] and powder-fed [27] DED deposits where layer height and heat input is greater. These bands were observed to have straight lines that are parallel to the deposition di­ rection for single-bead multi-layer [7,30] and curved lines for multi-bead  multi-layer  [9,28]  deposits.  Kobryn  and  Semiatin  [33] explained this banding in Ti alloys to be caused by the re-heating of the substrate just below the beta-Ti ( β ) transus temperature. Kelly et al. [27, 29]  studied  layer  banding  phenomenon  on  powder-fed  laser  metal deposition (LMD) of Ti -6Al -4V and reported a layer band-free zone with finer alpha-Ti ( α ) laths compared to the rest of the deposit, which was labeled as the transient zone and formed during the full β anneal of the final layer deposition. The rest of the deposit with regularly spaced layer bands  was  designated  as  the  steady-state  zone  [27,29].  The  micro­ structure in the steady-state zone consisted of α laths colonies along the layer bands and basket-weave morphology in between the layer bands [27,29]. Baufeld et al. studied laser wire-fed deposition (LWD) [26] and Zhu et al. [34] studied LMD of Ti -6Al -4V and both suggested that the reduction in α phase fraction at temperatures slightly below the β transus resulted  in  the  layer  banding  and  observed  secondary α laths  in  the bands. Ho et al. [22] investigated the compositional differences in the layer bands of Ti -6Al -4V produced by wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) and reported no segregation at the layer bands. Their study showed that cyclic heating and cooling did not result in any composi­ tional variation along the layer bands and the differences were purely morphological. Few studies also investigated the effect of the transient zone  and  layer  banding  on  mechanical  properties  [9,26,27,30].  For instance, Baufeld et al. [26] compared hardness in the transient and steady-state zone for both LWD and tungsten inert gas (TIG) deposition [26] and showed that these zones had similar hardness, unless when α ′ martensite  formed  in  the  transient  zone.  However,  a  knowledge  gap emerges from these few studies.  The mechanical property character­ ization of the transient zone and comparison with the steady-state zone has been limited to microhardness measurements, due to the limited size of the transient zone (i.e. upper 5 -15 layers of the deposit, depending on the process). Tensile characterization of these zones requires utilization of miniature tensile specimens, which are starting to emerge as a valid testing route. Such specimens have only been applied to electron beam melting  (EBM)  [35],  LPBF  [36],  LMD  [37]  systems  previously.  To address this knowledge gap, protocol for testing miniature specimens must be available.

texts.orig: In this study, small-scale mechanical testing was utilized to under­ stand the variation in microstructure and mechanical properties of an EB-WF deposited Ti -6Al -4V alloy. The miniature tensile test samples were  fully  extracted  from  the  transient  and  steady  state  regions  to determine similarities/differences in their tensile properties. The data was compared with a miniature wrought specimen (for which the me­ chanical  properties  from  E8  standard  [38]  specimen  testing  were known), as well as with AMS 4911P wrought [39] and ASTM F1108 cast [40] Ti -6Al -4V standards. Post fracture analysis of the tested specimens from the cross-section that is parallel to the loading direction as well as from the fracture surface was conducted to understand their respective deformation and fracture behaviors.

texts.orig: A 42 kW Sciaky EB-WF AM system was used to fabricate single bead Ti -6Al -4V thin wall deposits under 5 × 10 3 Pa (5 × 10 5 mbar) vac­ uum at the Aerospace Manufacturing Technologies Centre of the Na­ tional Research Council of Canada in Montreal, QC, Canada. Timetal Ti -6Al -4V (AMS4911P) wrought plate and Timetal Ti -6Al -4V (AMS 4954) wire with a 0.9 mm diameter were used for the deposition ex­ periments. The chemical compositions of the feedstock wire and sub­ strate  are  given  in  Table  1.  Substrate  plates  were  sectioned  to  have dimensions of 70 mm in width, 35 mm in height, and 3 mm in thickness, and  all  surfaces  were  machined.  The  rolling  direction  (RD)  of  the wrought  plate  was  aligned  parallel  to  the  build  direction  (BD).  The deposition was carried out with a travel speed and wire feed rate of 3.81 mm/s and 8.5 mm/s, respectively. The deposition direction (DD) was reversed after each successive layer. In addition, a waiting time of 35 s between layers was utilized to reduce heat accumulation on the coupon. A total of 50 consecutive layers (500 μ m layer thickness) were deposited to reach a build height of approximately 25 mm. The fabricated coupon was cooled down to room temperature under vacuum.

texts.orig: Fig. 1(a) shows the EB-WF deposited Ti -6Al -4V coupon. Two sets of specimen  geometries -namely  miniature  tensile  test  specimens  and microstructural/hardness analysis specimens -were then extracted from the coupons by electrical discharge machining (EDM). Dimensions and locations of these geometries can be seen in Fig. 1(b) and (c) . Linear (Ra) and areal (Sa) arithmetic mean heights of the miniature tensile speci­ mens ' surfaces were measured as 0.7 ± 0.2 μ m and 1.1 ± 0.2 μ m using a VK-X (Keyence, Mississauga, Canada) 3D laser scanning confocal/opti­ cal  microscope  (OM),  respectively.  The  microstructural  specimens (extracted  according  to  Fig.  1(b))  were  metallographically  prepared using an automated Tegramin 30 (Struers, Ballerup, Denmark) grinding/polishing system. Specimens were initially ground using 80, 240,  and  1200  grit  SiC  grinding  papers,  then  polished  with  a  9 μ m diamond suspension on a rigid composite disk followed by a 0.02 μ m silica suspension on a synthetic cloth. The texture and grain orientations of the specimens were analyzed by electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD)  using  a  Hitachi  SU3500  tungsten  filament  scanning  electron microscope (SEM) (Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan) with operating conditions of 15 kV voltage and 0.5 μ m step size. Pole figures were extracted from the EBSD data using a half width of 10 ◦ and cluster size of 5 ◦ .  Chemical etching  for  microstructural  examination  was  applied  using  Kroll ' s etchant  with 2  ml  HF,  10  ml  HNO3  and  88  ml  H2O.  The  previously mentioned OM and JCM-7000 NeoScope (Jeol, Peabody, USA) Benchtop SEM equipped with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) were used for metallographic and elemental investigations. Microstructural observa­ tions were used as a guideline to define the extent of the transient zone from the top of the deposit.

texts.orig: Fig.  2  illustrates  the  macro-  and  microstructure  of  the  EB-WF deposited Ti -6Al -4V coupons through a series of OM and SEM micro­ graphs at various magnifications. In the OM micrograph shown in Fig. 2 (a), two regions can be identified at low magnification: a lighter contrast transient zone and a darker contrast steady-state zone. The transient zone comprises roughly the last 12 layers, which is approximately the top  6  mm of  the  build  height  of  the  deposit.  The  remaining  portion underneath  is  labeled  as  the  steady-state  zone.  A  repetitive  banded structure was observed in the steady-state zone. These repeating ' layer bands ' are approximately 100 μ m wide and 500 μ m apart from each other  along  the  build  direction  and  appear  to  have  darker  contrast. Further examination shows the second type of banding structure with a lighter contrast and a curved shape. These bands are known as ' fusion bands ' [22]. Although layer bands are extensively characterized in the literature [9,26 -28], fusion bands were only observed a few times by Ho et al. [22] for WAAM and by Fachinotti et al. [42] for TIG produced Ti -6Al -4V.  Unlike  layer  bands,  fusion  bands  appear  to  be  repetitive throughout all build heights extending through both zones. Fig. 2(b) illustrates the mosaic assembly of SEM micrographs from the dashed rectangle at the interface between the transient and steady-state zones, as demarcated in Fig. 2(a). The transient and steady-state (inside bands & between bands) microstructures are shown at various magnifications in  this  figure.  The  transient  microstructure  contains  basket-weave morphology where α laths are in multiple orientations and separated by the β phase. In this zone α lath widths appear to be non-homogeneous, as some laths are visibly larger than the others. The steady-state zone starts with the first layer band from the top of the deposit. texts.orig: The  formation  of  the  banded  structure  depends  on  the  deposited layer  height  and  the  thermal  profile  generated  by  the  moving  heat source. Two effective transition temperatures that dictate the charac­ teristics of layer and fusion bands are the β -transus temperature (~1273 K) and the liquidus temperature (~1933 K), respectively [16]. Deposi­ tion of a new layer elevates the heat source position to a higher location. This consequently increments both the β -transus and liquidus isotherms upwards to a new position by an amount approximately equal to the layer height. Thus, the layer bands form where the temperature reaches just below the β -transus temperature, and partial β transformation re­ sults in α colony formation during cooling. The coarsening phenomenon in the steady-state zone has been also reported for other DED techniques [26,27,30,45]. Large dif­ ferences in α lath widths are commonly observed due to secondary α phase formation in titanium alloys [46,47]. For example, Baufeld et al. How­ ever,  since  secondary α formation  requires  partial β phase  trans­ formation and subsequent α transformation with cooling, it is thought that the thinner laths inside the transient zone are not secondary α laths in this work.

texts.orig: Fig.  4  shows  the  EBSD  grain  orientation  maps  acquired  from  the wrought substrate, the transient zone, and the steady state zone of an EB-WF deposited Ti -6Al -4V coupon. The grain boundaries are denoted as black lines in the maps for misorientations greater than 10 ◦ . Firstly, this Figure shows that the wrought microstructure had a typical bimodal morphology  with  equiaxed α grains.  The  pole  figure  reveals  this microstructure exhibits a texture (multiples of uniform density (mud) intensity of 8) with maxima near < 10 -11 > direction. This texture is related to the original thermomechanical process of the wrought sub­ strate  [48].  Secondly,  the  transient  zone  orientation  map  reveals basket-weave α laths that exhibit 6 possible crystallographic orienta­ tions  on  the  pole  figure  for  the  basal  plane.  These  orientations  are defined by Burger ' s relationship ({110} β //{0001} α ) during the allo­ tropic phase transformation during cooling. Six possible {110} planes of the BCC β phase would then transform to 6 possible {0001} basal planes of the HCP α phase. The pole figure for the basket-weave morphology thus shows 6 maxima (maximum intensity of 50) that are associated with initial β orientation. Multiple β grains create further possible ori­ entations and result in the multiple configuration variants of the α laths in  this  zone.  This  results  in  a  non-textured  structure  in  macroscopic scale. Lastly, the grain orientation map of the steady-state zone showed both α colony band and basket-weave morphologies. Colony islands are shown as a single grain in the grain orientation maps, due to the low angle  grain  boundaries  (LAGB)  ( < 10 ◦ )  between  the  constituent  indi­ vidual α laths  with  similar  crystallographic  orientations  [49].  Again, there are 6 possible crystallographic orientations for the colony islands, thus  a  similar ' random ' texture  with  larger  scales  is  present  for  the steady-state zone with colonies.

This slightly higher hardness in the transient zone is associated with the finer microstructure in this region, as previously shown. Although many studies reported the α lath width variance between the transient and steady-state zones of Ti -6Al -4V in literature [22,27,45], to our knowledge only Baufeld et al. [26] inves­ tigated  its  corresponding  effects  on  hardness  for  TIG  deposition  and LWD. Their results showed comparable hardness in both zones for TIG, but significantly higher hardness (100 Hv) in the transient zone for the LWD. However, this difference in the latter was attributed to  the α' martensite  formation  with  solid  solution  strengthening  [26].  Consid­ ering the lack of martensite formation in this study the observed smaller variation in the hardness can be explained by the lath size difference between the transient and steady-state zones. This explanation is more plausible considering their hardness results for TIG coupons [26]. Sec­ ondly, there was no evident hardness variation in the steady-state zone even when the morphology of the α laths alternated between colony and basket-weave at 500 μ m intervals. This is in good agreement with the findings of Kelly et al. [29] for LMD-built Ti -6Al -4V. Their hardness maps showed a homogeneous hardness profile within the steady-state zone with no distinct change at the layer band area [29]. This shows that hardness is mainly affected by the individual α lath size rather than collective morphology.

texts.orig: It is well known that strain hardening is associated with the gener­ ation,  multiplication  and  interactions  between  dislocations  [61,62]. Also, it has been shown that the dislocations in Ti -6Al -4V are prefer­ entially emitted from α / β interfaces and glide in prismatic, basal, and pyramidal planes of α laths [63]. Thus the difference observed in the stress-strain  curves  could  be  attributed  to  the  differences  in α lath morphologies.  To  investigate  this  further,  Schmid  factor  (SF)  fre­ quencies for basal, prismatic, and pyramidal slips of the HCP α phase were calculated from the undeformed EBSD grain orientation maps for each microstructural zone in Fig. 4, and Σ SF ( > 0.4) values were reported in Fig. 7(a). SF describes the slip plane and slip direction in a material that can resolve the highest shear stress. A higher SF means that this specific slip system will be preferentially activated during deformation [64,65].  It  can  be  seen  that  for  both  wrought  and  steady-state  zone (colony) Σ SF ( > 0.4) values for pyramidal slip were higher, which in­ dicates  pyramidal  slip  is  more  active  than  basal  and  prismatic  slip. However, for  the  transient  zone  with  basket-weave  morphology,  the basal slip shows higher Σ SF ( > 0.4) value compared to pyramidal and prismatic  slip.  Furthermore,  the  transient  zone  in  general  showed  a lower Σ SF ( > 0.4) fraction compared to others. Lower overall SF could qualitatively imply the deformation-induced realignment of the laths are more difficult [64 -66]. Ullah et al. [65] previously showed that α laths with low SF ( < 0.4) would deform by splitting into smaller laths with an evident increase in LAGB fraction. On the other hand, α laths with higher SF ( > 0.4) would deform by grain reorientation rather than grain split­ ting [65]. Thus, it is expected that the deformation by grain splitting would be more evident in the transient zone due to its lower calculated Σ SF ( > 0.4) fractions.

texts.orig: These investigations highlight that even if tensile properties or lath dimensions are mostly similar for the transient and steady-state zones of the EB-WF deposits, their thermal histories, consequent microstructure morphologies and deformation mechanisms are different. These differ­ ences could be possibly dismissed as non-significant for EB-WF deposits or even could be viewed as an advantage to eliminate the need for ho­ mogenization heat treatments. But it should be noted that such hetero­ geneities  could  be  more  significant  depending  on  the  geometry  or process type. For example, the mechanical properties of the laser based DED techniques could be more affected, since higher dislocation den­ sities and larger microstructural variations could be expected within the transient  zone.  Thus  understanding  these  process  related  differences within the build volume are critical for Ti -6Al -4V.

The  average dimple size for the wrought, transient zone, and steady-state zone are measured as 4.6 ± 1.3 μ m, 5.2 ± 1.2 μ m, and 5.1 ± 1.5 μ m, respectively. It is well established that the main failure mechanism of the Ti -6Al -4V alloy involves crack formation and progression through microvoid formation, growth,  and  coalescence  [1,2,70].  Previous  works  showed  that  the microvoid formation preferentially occurs at the α / β interfaces due to the strength difference and strain incompatibility between α laths and β matrix  [44,71].  Although  no  general  quantification  exists,  uniformly distributed fine and deep dimpled structures are usually associated with a high degree of ductility in titanium alloys [72].
